Q000747:
Why this is correct:
Memory and disk usage are OS-level metrics that EC2 doesn't report by default. The CloudWatch agent collects and publishes them.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Subscription filter: logs.
• Detailed monitoring: more frequent default metrics, not memory.
• CloudTrail: API calls.

Key takeaway: OS metrics → CloudWatch agent.
Q000748:
Why this is correct:
CloudTrail records AWS API activity for auditing. CloudWatch Logs stores application and system logs.

Why the other options are wrong:
• S3 requirement swapped: incorrect.
• Roles reversed: incorrect.
• Interchangeable: no.

Key takeaway: CloudTrail = who did what; CloudWatch Logs = app logs.
Q000749:
Why this is correct:
The instance role must include cloudwatch:PutMetricData (for example, via CloudWatchAgentServerPolicy) for the agent to publish metrics.

Why the other options are wrong:
• NAT gateway: only if no route to endpoints; not indicated.
• Legacy agent: no.
• Instance type: no.

Key takeaway: agent metrics missing → role permissions.
Q000750:
Why this is correct:
Amazon Managed Service for Prometheus stores and queries Prometheus metrics without running Prometheus servers, fitting existing instrumentation.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Managed Grafana: visualization, not storage.
• X-Ray: traces.
• Container Insights only: doesn't use existing Prometheus setup directly.

Key takeaway: managed Prometheus metrics → AMP.
Q000751:
Why this is correct:
CloudWatch cross-account observability with a monitoring account gives one view of metrics, logs, and traces from many accounts and Regions.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Log replication: logs only.
• Merging dashboard JSON: manual.
• Config aggregator: configuration.

Key takeaway: multi-account monitoring → cross-account observability.
Q000752:
Why this is correct:
Container Insights collects CPU, memory, and other metrics for ECS and EKS at the cluster, service, and task or pod levels.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Trusted Advisor, X-Ray, Flow Logs: not container metrics.

Key takeaway: container metrics → Container Insights.
Q000753:
Why this is correct:
On EKS, Container Insights needs the CloudWatch agent (Observability add-on) DaemonSet running on nodes. Without it, node metrics don't appear.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Upgrade Kubernetes: not required.
• Reinstall CNI: unrelated.
• Identity Center: unrelated.

Key takeaway: EKS Container Insights → deploy the agent DaemonSet.
Q000756:
Why this is correct:
An EventBridge rule on the alarm's state change can start the remediation runbook (for example, restarting the app) automatically.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Manual runbook: slow.
• Config remediation: for configuration compliance.
• Alarm reboot action: reboots the whole instance rather than running the runbook.

Key takeaway: alarm-driven automation → EventBridge.
Q000757:
Why this is correct:
A Config remediation action running an SSM runbook can automatically fix noncompliant resources (for example, snapshot and replace with encrypted volumes, or notify).

Why the other options are wrong:
• Conformance packs alone: detect only.
• CloudTrail Insights: anomalies.
• Daily manual review: slow.

Key takeaway: auto-fix compliance → Config remediation.
Q000758:
Why this is correct:
If the rule fires but instances don't stop, check that the Lambda execution role allows ec2:StopInstances.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Cron syntax: rule wouldn't fire at all.
• Detailed monitoring: unrelated.
• Log retention: unrelated.

Key takeaway: automation failures → check permissions.
Q000759:
Why this is correct:
An input transformer reshapes the event into the payload the target expects.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Schema registry: describes events.
• Bus resource policy: permissions.
• DLQ: failures.

Key takeaway: reshape events → input transformer.
Q000760:
Why this is correct:
A CloudWatch alarm on StatusCheckFailed_System with the recover action moves the instance to healthy hardware automatically.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Trusted Advisor: no actions.
• RebootInstances: doesn't fix hardware issues.
• Config-triggered runbook: indirect.

Key takeaway: system check failures → recover action.
Q000762:
Why this is correct:
If the rule never fires, its event pattern likely doesn't match the alarm event's source (aws.cloudwatch) or detail-type (CloudWatch Alarm State Change).

Why the other options are wrong:
• Low timeout: function would start.
• Can't target Lambda: it can.
• Alarms don't emit events: they do.

Key takeaway: rule not firing → check the event pattern.
Q000763:
Why this is correct:
Patch Manager with a patch baseline and maintenance window installs missing critical patches automatically and reports compliance.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Session Manager manual patching: slow.
• Inventory: lists software only.
• Parameter Store: storage only.

Key takeaway: automated patching → Patch Manager.
Q000764:
Why this is correct:
One EventBridge rule can have up to five targets, invoking them concurrently from a single event.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Step Functions only: unnecessary.
• Three alarms: duplication.
• One Lambda calling all: coupled.

Key takeaway: fan out one event → multiple rule targets.
Q000766:
Why this is correct:
Multipart upload is required for objects over 5 GB in a single PUT and recommended above 100 MB, uploading parts in parallel with retries.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Batch Operations: bulk actions on existing objects.
• S3 Select: queries.
• Single PUT: limited to 5 GB.

Key takeaway: large uploads → multipart.
Q000767:
Why this is correct:
FSx for Windows File Server provides SMB shares with Windows ACLs and Active Directory integration.

Why the other options are wrong:
• EFS: NFS.
• FSx for Lustre: HPC.
• S3: object storage.

Key takeaway: Windows SMB → FSx for Windows.
Q000768:
Why this is correct:
Performance Insights shows database load by wait events and top SQL, helping diagnose intermittent slow queries.

Why the other options are wrong:
• X-Ray: application traces.
• Flow Logs: network.
• Basic metrics only: no query detail.

Key takeaway: slow queries → Performance Insights.
Q000769:
Why this is correct:
A cluster placement group places instances close together in one AZ for the lowest latency and highest throughput between them.

Why the other options are wrong:
• No placement group: less predictable.
• Partition: fault isolation.
• Spread: separates instances.

Key takeaway: tightly coupled HPC → cluster placement.
Q000770:
Why this is correct:
A partition placement group separates groups of instances onto different racks, matching rack-aware replica placement.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Spread: small number of instances.
• Single AZ without group: no rack control.
• Cluster: same rack risk.

Key takeaway: rack-aware distributed stores → partition placement.
Q000771:
Why this is correct:
Burstable t3 instances slow down when CPU credits are exhausted. Use unlimited mode or a larger or non-burstable type.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Placement group: unrelated.
• Route table: unrelated.
• EBS size: not the pattern.

Key takeaway: periodic T-instance slowdowns → CPU credits.
Q000773:
Why this is correct:
DynamoDB auto scaling (Application Auto Scaling) adjusts provisioned capacity, and a scheduled action can raise capacity before the predictable morning spike.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Manual script: toil.
• Switch to RDS: unrelated.
• DAX: reads only.

Key takeaway: predictable DynamoDB load → auto scaling.
Q000775:
Why this is correct:
Using versioned object keys (for example, image-v2.png) and updating references makes CloudFront fetch the new object immediately without invalidations.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Price class: edge locations.
• Versioning retention: unrelated.
• Disable caching: loses performance.

Key takeaway: cache busting → versioned names.
Q000776:
Why this is correct:
Aurora Auto Scaling adds and removes Aurora Replicas based on load, matching variable read traffic.

Why the other options are wrong:
• RDS Proxy: connections.
• Multi-AZ readable standbys: fixed count.
• Global Database: multi-Region.

Key takeaway: variable Aurora reads → replica auto scaling.
Q000777:
Why this is correct:
Predictive scaling forecasts traffic and scales ahead of time, avoiding the lag of reactive scaling.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Scheduled: fixed times only.
• Simple with cooldown: still reactive.
• Target tracking: reactive.

Key takeaway: scale ahead of spikes → predictive scaling.
Q000778:
Why this is correct:
Cluster mode enabled shards data across multiple node groups, scaling writes and memory beyond a single primary.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Multi-AZ on single shard: availability only.
• Longer TTL: more memory use.
• Larger node with cluster mode disabled: still one primary.

Key takeaway: scale Redis writes → cluster mode with shards.
Q000780:
Why this is correct:
Read replicas use asynchronous replication and serve reads. A Multi-AZ standby uses synchronous replication for failover and doesn't serve reads (in the instance deployment).

Why the other options are wrong:
• Same feature: no.
• Replicas auto-failover: not automatic.
• Standby serves reads: not in Multi-AZ DB instances.

Key takeaway: replicas scale reads; Multi-AZ provides failover.
Q000781:
Why this is correct:
Route 53 health checkers run outside the VPC and can't reach an internal ALB. Use a CloudWatch alarm-based health check instead.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Interval too short: no.
• ALBs unsupported: public ALBs are supported.
• Auto-disabled: no.

Key takeaway: private resources → alarm-based health checks.
Q000782:
Why this is correct:
Cross-zone load balancing spreads requests evenly across all registered targets in all AZs, even when AZs have different target counts.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Connection draining: deregistration.
• Sticky sessions: affinity.
• Slow start: warm-up.

Key takeaway: uneven targets per AZ → cross-zone.
Q000783:
Why this is correct:
Weighted routing with health checks splits traffic between stacks and stops sending traffic to an unhealthy one.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Geoproximity bias 0: location-based.
• Latency without health checks: no failover.
• Simple with two A records: no health awareness.

Key takeaway: active-active split with failover → weighted + health checks.
Q000784:
Why this is correct:
Multi-AZ survives AZ outages, at the cost of some cross-AZ data transfer and latency.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Single-AZ better: no.
• Multi-AZ removes transfer costs: adds them.
• Zero downtime always: no guarantee.

Key takeaway: multi-AZ = resilience with some cost.
Q000785:
Why this is correct:
RDS updates the endpoint's DNS record during failover. Apps that cache the old IP beyond the TTL keep failing until they re-resolve.

Why the other options are wrong:
• DNS not updated: it is.
• 24 hours: typically minutes.
• Same AZ standby: not possible.

Key takeaway: honor DNS TTLs after failover.
Q000786:
Why this is correct:
Automated backups with transaction logs support point-in-time restore to any second within the retention period.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Identical to snapshots: snapshots restore to their creation time.
• Aurora only: RDS supports PITR.
• Reversed: incorrect.

Key takeaway: restore to a precise time → PITR.
Q000788:
Why this is correct:
Versioning keeps prior versions, and MFA Delete requires MFA to permanently delete versions or change versioning state.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Object Lambda: transforms reads.
• Transfer Acceleration: speed.
• Intelligent-Tiering: cost.

Key takeaway: prevent permanent deletion → versioning + MFA Delete.
Q000789:
Why this is correct:
Versioning protects against overwrites and deletes within a bucket. CRR adds a copy in another Region for DR. They complement each other.

Why the other options are wrong:
• CRR removes versioning need: CRR requires versioning.
• Identical protection: no.
• Reversed roles: incorrect.

Key takeaway: versioning + CRR = recovery + Regional copy.
Q000790:
Why this is correct:
AWS Backup or FSx's automatic daily backups provide managed, consistent backups of FSx for Windows file systems.

Why the other options are wrong:
• EBS snapshots: FSx doesn't expose volumes.
• S3 versioning on FSx: not applicable.
• CLI copies: unmanaged.

Key takeaway: FSx backups → AWS Backup or FSx backups.
Q000791:
Why this is correct:
Warm standby runs a scaled-down working copy: faster than pilot light and cheaper than active-active, but slower than active-active.

Why the other options are wrong:
• No compute running: that's pilot light-ish.
• Active-active slower: no.
• Identical: no.

Key takeaway: DR strategies trade cost for recovery speed.
Q000792:
Why this is correct:
The AWS Backup service role needs permissions for each resource type, such as creating RDS snapshots. Missing permissions fail those jobs.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Different VPC: irrelevant.
• One type per plan: no.
• RDS unsupported: supported.

Key takeaway: backup failures by resource type → role permissions.
Q000794:
Why this is correct:
An EC2 Image Builder container recipe pipeline rebuilds the hardened image on a schedule, runs tests, and pushes it to ECR.

Why the other options are wrong:
• CodeDeploy redeploy: doesn't rebuild images.
• Manual rebuilds: inconsistent.
• S3 lifecycle: not a build trigger.

Key takeaway: automated hardened images → Image Builder.
Q000797:
Why this is correct:
The CDK synthesizes CloudFormation templates from code, and CloudFormation provisions the resources.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Replaces CloudFormation: uses it.
• Only serverless: no.
• CloudFormation inside CDK: reversed.

Key takeaway: CDK → CloudFormation templates.
Q000798:
Why this is correct:
If instance launches fail in an existing subnet, the subnet may have run out of available IP addresses.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Missing RunInstances: fails from the start, not after working.
• Deleted AMI: possible, but the scenario points to capacity growth.
• SG rule limit: doesn't block launches.

Key takeaway: launch failures in busy subnets → IP exhaustion.
Q000799:
Why this is correct:
Two resources referencing each other create a cycle. Remove the mutual reference and create the association as a separate resource (for example, a separate security group ingress rule).

Why the other options are wrong:
• Split stacks with cross-references: still circular.
• DependsOn on each other: still circular.
• Longer timeout: no.

Key takeaway: break cycles with standalone association resources.
Q000800:
Why this is correct:
When a stack uses a service role, CloudFormation acts with that role's permissions. It needs iam:CreateRole to create IAM roles.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Metadata grants: no.
• Expired policy: policies don't expire.
• Can't create IAM: it can with CAPABILITY_IAM.

Key takeaway: service role must allow what the template creates.
Q000802:
Why this is correct:
A service-managed StackSet with automatic deployment targets the OU and deploys to all current and new accounts and chosen Regions.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Manual deployment: toil.
• Config aggregators: can't deploy.
• Service Catalog per owner: inconsistent.

Key takeaway: org-wide baselines → StackSets.
Q000803:
Why this is correct:
RAM shares a single resource with other accounts. StackSets deploys separate copies of resources to each account and Region.

Why the other options are wrong:
• StackSets one account: deploys to many.
• RAM uses templates: no.
• Interchangeable: different.

Key takeaway: share one vs. deploy many copies.
Q000805:
Why this is correct:
CloudFormation is AWS-native and manages state for you (no state file), but it isn't multi-cloud like Terraform.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Terraform state managed by AWS: no.
• Terraform no VCS: false.
• CloudFormation needs state backend: no.

Key takeaway: CloudFormation = managed state, AWS-only.
Q000807:
Why this is correct:
A Config rule with a remediation action running an SSM runbook (for example, a patching runbook) remediates flagged instances automatically.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Inspector launching instances: no.
• Manual scans: slow.
• Log search and email: no remediation.

Key takeaway: auto-remediate noncompliant instances → Config + SSM.
Q000808:
Why this is correct:
Run Command runs commands ad hoc on instances. Automation orchestrates multi-step workflows across AWS resources.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Target restrictions: no.
• Run Command requires Lambda: no.
• Same feature: no.

Key takeaway: one-off commands vs. orchestrated runbooks.
Q000809:
Why this is correct:
State Manager associations continuously apply and maintain a desired configuration on instances on a schedule.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Distributor: package distribution.
• Session Manager: shell access.
• One-time Automation: not continuous.

Key takeaway: keep instances in desired state → State Manager.
Q000810:
Why this is correct:
The Automation execution role lacks ec2:RebootInstances, so that step fails with access denied.

Why the other options are wrong:
• OS blocks API: no.
• Root credentials: no.
• Deprecated document: no.

Key takeaway: Automation failures → execution role permissions.
Q000812:
Why this is correct:
An EventBridge rule on the RunInstances CloudTrail event triggers a Lambda function that tags each new instance with the creator's identity.

Why the other options are wrong:
• S3 notification: unrelated to EC2.
• Launch wizard field: unreliable.
• Hourly Run Command: delayed.

Key takeaway: auto-tag on creation → EventBridge + CloudTrail event.
Q000813:
Why this is correct:
Sending S3 events to EventBridge adds rich filtering, multiple targets per rule, and archive and replay.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Direct notifications more targets: fewer.
• 90-day replay by default: no.
• EventBridge can't use S3: it can.

Key takeaway: complex S3 event routing → EventBridge.
Q000814:
Why this is correct:
If the rule matches but the function never runs, the function's resource-based policy may not allow EventBridge (events.amazonaws.com) to invoke it.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Deprecated runtime: different error.
• Too broad pattern: would over-trigger.
• Low memory: function would still start.

Key takeaway: EventBridge → Lambda needs invoke permission.
Q000816:
Why this is correct:
EventBridge needs an IAM role with permission (for example, ssm:StartAutomationExecution) to start the Automation runbook target.

Why the other options are wrong:
• S3 bucket policy: unrelated.
• Local time cron: EventBridge rules use UTC, but the rule fires; the target fails.
• SSM Agent: only for commands on instances.

Key takeaway: rule targets need role permissions.
Q000817:
Why this is correct:
A scheduled Automation runbook with an approval step finds unattached volumes and deletes them only after approval.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Budgets alert: no cleanup.
• Manual nightly review: toil.
• S3 lifecycle: EBS isn't S3.

Key takeaway: safe automated cleanup → runbook with approval.
Q000818:
Why this is correct:
EventBridge rules on DevOps Guru insight events can route to Lambda or SSM runbooks for automated responses.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Polling API with cron: inefficient.
• RDS triggers: overcomplicated.
• Built-in auto-remediation: not a DevOps Guru feature.

Key takeaway: act on insights → EventBridge.
Q000821:
Why this is correct:
Log file integrity validation uses signed digest files to detect whether log files were modified or deleted.

Why the other options are wrong:
• CloudTrail Lake: querying.
• SSE-KMS: encryption, not tamper detection.
• Insights: anomalies.

Key takeaway: tamper detection → integrity validation.
Q000823:
Why this is correct:
The IAM Policy Simulator evaluates policies for a principal and action to show whether and why access is allowed or denied.

Why the other options are wrong:
• CloudTrail Lake: history.
• Config history: configuration.
• Inspector reachability: network.

Key takeaway: debug permissions → Policy Simulator.
Q000824:
Why this is correct:
Separate OUs for production and development let different SCPs and guardrails apply to each.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Identity Center instead: different purpose.
• Separate organizations: extra overhead.
• All under root: no differentiation.

Key takeaway: environment separation → OUs.
Q000827:
Why this is correct:
A conformance pack bundles Config rules and remediations to demonstrate compliance with a baseline and can be deployed across accounts.

Why the other options are wrong:
• One custom rule: not a baseline.
• Multiple delivery channels: not supported this way.
• Aggregator authorization: data collection.

Key takeaway: compliance baselines → conformance packs.
Q000828:
Why this is correct:
A single multi-Region trail logs events in all Regions, including new ones, to one destination.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Config aggregators: not CloudTrail.
• Per-Region trails: more work.
• Insights without a trail: requires a trail.

Key takeaway: all Regions → multi-Region trail.
Q000831:
Why this is correct:
If rotation fails, the rotation function may not reach the secret endpoint or database, or lacks permission to update the password, leaving mismatched credentials.

Why the other options are wrong:
• KMS rotation: unrelated.
• IAM role vs. username: unrelated.
• No DB rotation support: supported.

Key takeaway: rotation failures → function network and permissions.
Q000832:
Why this is correct:
SSHBruteForce means repeated failed SSH logins from a suspicious source. Tighten SSH access (restrict or remove port 22, use Session Manager).

Why the other options are wrong:
• Excessive role permissions: different finding.
• Missing conformance pack: unrelated.
• Unencrypted volume: unrelated.
• Trail stopped: different finding.

Key takeaway: brute force → restrict SSH exposure.
Q000835:
Why this is correct:
NACL rules are evaluated lowest number first. A broad deny at a lower number can also block ephemeral return traffic for legitimate flows.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Random order: no.
• Can't mix allow and deny: they can.
• Security group now blocking: unchanged.

Key takeaway: check what a new NACL deny actually matches.
Q000837:
Why this is correct:
AWS Network Firewall provides stateful inspection and intrusion prevention with Suricata-compatible signatures.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Shield Standard: DDoS.
• GuardDuty: detection.
• WAF: HTTP-layer filtering.

Key takeaway: VPC IPS → Network Firewall.
Q000839:
Why this is correct:
Latency-based routing sends each user to the Region with the lowest latency among the three.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Geolocation: by country, not performance.
• Multivalue: random healthy answers.
• Simple with three IPs: no latency awareness.

Key takeaway: best performance globally → latency routing.
Q000840:
Why this is correct:
Geolocation routing directs users by country to a specific endpoint, meeting compliance requirements.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Latency: may route elsewhere.
• Multivalue: random.
• Weighted: proportional.

Key takeaway: country-based routing → geolocation.
Q000842:
Why this is correct:
An outbound endpoint with forwarding rules resolves on-premises names from the VPC, and an inbound endpoint lets on-premises DNS resolve AWS private names.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Public zone: exposure.
• Outbound only: one direction.
• DX handles DNS: no.

Key takeaway: bidirectional hybrid DNS → inbound + outbound endpoints.
Q000843:
Why this is correct:
A CloudFront origin group with status-code-based failover switches to a secondary origin when the primary fails.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Route 53 to ALB: bypasses CloudFront.
• Custom error redirect: clunky.
• Two distributions: complex.

Key takeaway: CloudFront origin failover → origin groups.
Q000845:
Why this is correct:
A Resolver forwarding rule applies only to VPCs it's associated with. Check that the rule is associated with the instances' VPC.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Public zone: not needed.
• Public IPs: not needed.
• CloudFront: unrelated.

Key takeaway: rules must be associated with VPCs.
Q000847:
Why this is correct:
Outbound requests succeed, so routing works. Responses return to ephemeral ports, which a stateless NACL must allow inbound.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Missing NAT route: requests would fail.
• Elastic IPs: not needed behind NAT.
• SG outbound rule: SGs are stateful.

Key takeaway: NACLs need return-port rules.
Q000848:
Why this is correct:
A REJECT record in flow logs means a security group or NACL denied the traffic.

Why the other options are wrong:
• HTTP 4xx: flow logs don't see HTTP.
• CPU credits: not a rejection.
• Wrong AZ: not a flow log status.

Key takeaway: REJECT = SG or NACL denial.
Q000849:
Why this is correct:
If VPC-A can't reach VPC-B, the TGW route table associated with A likely lacks B's route (missing association or propagation).

Why the other options are wrong:
• Overlapping CIDRs: not indicated.
• Two-VPC limit: no.
• Peering required: no.

Key takeaway: TGW connectivity = association + propagation.
Q000851:
Why this is correct:
New VPC CIDRs must be advertised over BGP and propagated to route tables. Otherwise on-premises can't reach them.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Two-subnet limit: no.
• Recreate VGW: no.
• BGP unsupported: supported.

Key takeaway: new CIDRs need advertisement and propagation.
Q000852:
Why this is correct:
CloudFront access logs show which requests got 502s, and ALB access logs show whether the origin returned the error.

Why the other options are wrong:
• DNS logs: not 502 causes.
• WAF logs only: not always WAF.
• Flow logs: no HTTP codes.

Key takeaway: trace 502s through each layer's logs.
Q002112:
Why this is correct:
EC2 doesn't publish memory metrics by default. The CloudWatch agent publishes memory utilization so you can alarm on it.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Detailed monitoring: no memory metrics.
• CPU as proxy: inaccurate.
• Flow logs: network.

Key takeaway: memory alarms → CloudWatch agent.
Q002113:
Why this is correct:
Anomaly detection alarms learn hourly and weekly patterns and alert when values leave the expected band.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Maximum statistic: doesn't handle seasonality.
• Higher static threshold: misses issues.
• Disable off-hours: blind spots.

Key takeaway: seasonal metrics → anomaly detection.
Q002114:
Why this is correct:
Performance Insights shows which SQL statements drive database load and waits.

Why the other options are wrong:
• CPU metric: no query detail.
• Enhanced Monitoring: OS metrics.
• Trusted Advisor: no.

Key takeaway: which SQL is expensive → Performance Insights.
Q002115:
Why this is correct:
Compute Optimizer recommends right-sizing, and including memory metrics from the CloudWatch agent makes recommendations more accurate.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Inspector: vulnerabilities.
• Pricing Calculator: estimates.
• Budgets: spend alerts.

Key takeaway: right-sizing → Compute Optimizer + memory metrics.
Q002116:
Why this is correct:
With the health check type set to ELB, the Auto Scaling group replaces instances that fail load balancer health checks, even if EC2 status checks pass.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Detailed monitoring: metrics only.
• Cross-zone: unrelated.
• Idle timeout: unrelated.

Key takeaway: replace app-unhealthy instances → ELB health checks.
Q002117:
Why this is correct:
An AWS Backup plan with cross-Region and cross-account copy rules to a vault protected by Vault Lock meets copy and immutability requirements.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Tags: not protection.
• S3 Versioning: not for EC2/EBS/RDS.
• Nightly scripts: fragile.

Key takeaway: protected cross-account backups → Backup + Vault Lock.
Q002118:
Why this is correct:
Point-in-time restore to 14:04 creates a new instance with the data as of that time.

Why the other options are wrong:
• In-place restore: not supported.
• Promote replica: replica also has the deletion.
• Reboot with failover: same data.

Key takeaway: undo accidental deletes → PITR to a new instance.
Q002119:
Why this is correct:
EFS with mount targets in each AZ provides a shared file system for instances across all three AZs.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Instance store with rsync: fragile.
• EBS shared over NFS: single point of failure.
• io2 Multi-Attach across AZs: single AZ only.

Key takeaway: shared files across AZs → EFS.
Q002120:
Why this is correct:
Patch Manager with baselines that auto-approve security updates after a delay, maintenance windows, and compliance reporting handles 800 instances.

Why the other options are wrong:
• User data on boot: uncontrolled.
• Manual: toil.
• Weekly AMI replacement: heavy for this.

Key takeaway: fleet patching → Patch Manager.
Q002121:
Why this is correct:
A CreationPolicy with cfn-signal makes CloudFormation wait for the instance to signal success after user data finishes.

Why the other options are wrong:
• DeletionPolicy: deletion.
